title: Storytelling, from prehistoric caves to modern cinemas

passage.title: Storytelling, from prehistoric caves to modern cinemas

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: It was told, we suppose, to people crouched around a fire: a tale of adventure, most likely – relating perhaps a remarkable hunt, an escape from mortal danger, or something else out of the ordinary. Whatever its thread, the weaving of this story was done with a prime purpose. The listeners must keep listening. They must not fall asleep. So, as the story went on, its audience should be sustained by one question above all: What happens next?

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first fireside stories in human history can never be known. They were kept in the heads of those who told them. This method of storage is not necessarily inefficient. From documented oral traditions in Australia and elsewhere we know that specialised storytellers and poets can recite from memory literally thousands of lines, in verse or prose, word for word. But while memory is rightly considered an art in itself, it is clear that a primary purpose of making signs is to have a system of reminders or mnemonic cues – signs that help us to recall certain information in the mind's eye. For example, in some Polynesian communities a notched memory stick may be used to help to guide a storyteller through successive stages of recitation.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: But in other parts of the world, the activity of storytelling historically resulted in the development or even the invention of writing systems. One theory about the arrival of literacy in ancient Greece, for example, argues that the epic tales traditionally attributed to Homer, a storyteller of the eighth century BC, were just so enchanting to hear that they had to be preserved. So the Greeks borrowed an alphabet from their neighbours in the eastern Mediterranean, the Phoenicians.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The custom of recording stories can be found around the world, from the archives of ancient Egypt which were written on paper derived from papyrus plants, to the scrolls made from the bark of trees on which the North American Ojibway Indians set down their creation myth. It is a well tried and universal practice: so much so that to this day storytime is probably most often associated with words on paper. Nowadays the formal practice of narrating a story aloud would seem – so we assume – to have given way to newspapers, novels and comic strips. This, however, is not the case. Statistically it is doubtful that the majority of humans currently rely upon the written word to get access to stories. So what is the alternative source?

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Each year, millions of people across the world go to the cinema, now the supreme storyteller. Any account of visual storytelling must begin with the recognition that a 'good story' relies upon formal patterns of plot and characterisation that have been embedded in the practice of storytelling over many generations.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Aspiring screenwriters really need look no further for essential advice than the fourth century BC Greek philosopher Aristotle. He left some incomplete lecture notes on the art of telling stories in various literary and dramatic modes, a slim volume known as Poetics. Though he can never have imagined a modern cinema, Aristotle is very accurate about the key elements required to get the crowds flocking to such a cultural centre. He analysed the process with cool rationalism. When a story enchants us, we lose the sense of where we are; we are drawn into the story so thoroughly that we forget it is a story being told, and react as though it is real. This is, in Aristotle's phrase, "the suspension of disbelief". We know the feeling. If we ever have stayed in our seats, stunned with grief, as the credits roll by, or for days after seeing that vivid evocation of horror have kept looking over our shoulders, then we have suspended disbelief. We have been caught in the storyteller's web. Did it all really happen? We really thought so—for a while.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Aristotle must have witnessed this experience often enough. He taught in Athens, the city where theatre developed as a primary form of civic ritual and recreation. Two theatrical types of storytelling, tragedy and comedy, caused Athenian audiences to lose themselves in sadness and laughter respectively. Tragedy, for Aristotle, was particularly potent in its capacity to enlist and then purge the emotions of those watching the story unfold on the stage, so he tried to identify those factors in the storyteller's art that brought about such engagement. For analysis he had not only the masterpieces of classical Greek tragedy, but also Homer, whose Iliad and Odyssey were already considered landmarks—stories by which all other stories should be measured. So, what was the secret of Homer's narrative art?

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: It was not hard to find. Homer created credible heroes. His heroes belonged to the past, they were mighty and magnificent, yet they were not fantasy figures. Homer reported the speeches of his heroes as if he had heard them himself. He made his heroes sulk, argue, cheat, and cry. They were, in short, people who seemed real, though in a story, and audiences could care about them, follow them, and want to know what happened to them next. As Aristotle saw, the hero who shows some weaknesses is intrinsically dramatic.
